accuracy.evidence: Register is presented as a choice driven by audience, purpose and context, as in CCSS L.3.3b, L.4.3c and SL.4.6 and the UK KS2 grammar appendix on formal and informal speech and writing. Contractions are correctly described as correct but informal, “May I” and “borrow” are standard formal swaps, and letter conventions such as Dear and Yours sincerely are kept to written letters rather than speech.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs that informal English is simply wrong, that formal means longer or more words, that capitals make a request formal, that contractions are spelling mistakes, that text speak is acceptable in school writing, and that letter phrases belong in a spoken class talk.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are specific to register: tapping chatty word tiles in a note to a teacher, a two-way word swapper with a chatty-to-formal bar used once towards formal and once back to informal, tapping contractions to expand them in a council letter, and dragging four speaking and writing situations into a formality ladder. No other flag lab uses word-level register swapping.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step isolates one part of the skill: spotting informal features, rewriting for a senior reader, showing that formal words to a friend sound stiff, handling contractions in formal writing, and extending the idea to speech by ranking a chat, a shop request, a class talk and a letter to the mayor.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions come before the action: which word makes a note chatty, whether informal English is wrong, and whether “I’m” or “I am” suits a council letter. The wrong options match beliefs children commonly hold, and the following task shows the answer in context.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions cover a headteacher note, a text to a friend, a formal request, contractions, a class talk and when informal fits. Each wrong option has its own message, such as capitals looking like shouting or Dear and yours sincerely belonging only in letters.

readability.evidence: Learner text uses short sentences and familiar words for ages 7 to 10, with examples quoted in place of grammar terms. Lab labels are a few words long, the meter reads simply Chatty and Formal, and feedback stays to one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph teaches a feature or a decision rule: chatty features, formal features, and the who, why and where questions. Prompts and lab copy contain no greetings, scene-setting or empty praise.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 and a 360 px Android viewport in light and dark themes: word tiles wrap onto new lines and are at least 40 px tall, the ladder cards span most of the width for easy dragging, and every action also has a full-width button below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Each canvas action has a labelled button twin (word taps, swaps with both words named, expansions, move up and down). The canvas aria-label reads out the whole current sentence or ladder order after every change, and the axe scan is clean in both themes.
